paragraphs.text: 上古之世，人民少而禽獸眾，人民不勝禽獸蟲蛇，有聖人作，搆木為巢以避群害，而民悅之，使王天下，號曰有巢氏。民食果蓏蚌蛤，腥臊惡臭而傷害腹胃，民多疾病，有聖人作，鑽燧取火以化腥臊，而民說之，使王天下，號之曰燧人氏。中古之世，天下大水，而鯀、禹決瀆。近古之世，桀、紂暴亂，而湯、武征伐。今有搆木鑽燧於夏后氏之世者，必為鯀、禹笑矣。有決瀆於殷、周之世者，必為湯、武笑矣。然則今有美堯、舜、湯、武、禹之道於當今之世者，必為新聖笑矣。是以聖人不期脩古，不法常可，論世之事，因為之備。宋人有耕田者，田中有株，兔走，觸株折頸而死，因釋其耒而守株，冀復得兔，兔不可復得，而身為宋國笑。今欲以先王之政，治當世之民，皆守株之類也。

In the ancient times, there were few people and many birds and beasts; the people could not contend with these creatures. A sage arose who built wooden nests in trees to avoid all dangers. The people rejoiced at this and made him king of the world. He was called Youchao Shi (the Nest Builder). The people ate fruits, melons, clams, and shellfish, which had foul and putrid odors that harmed their stomachs. Many people fell ill as a result. A sage arose who drilled wood to create fire in order to eliminate the foul smells. The people were pleased with this and made him king of theworld. He was called Sui Ren Shi (the Fire Drill Man). In the middle ancient times, there was a great flood across the world, and Gun and Yu took action to dredge the waterways. In the recent ancient times, Jie and Zhou were tyrannical and chaotic, and Tang and Wu launched military campaigns against them. If someone today built wooden nests or drilled for fire during the time of the Xia Hou Shi, he would surely be laughed at by Gun and Yu. If someone dredged waterways in the Shang or Zhou dynasties, he would surely be ridiculed by Tang and Wu. Yet if someone today praises the ways of Yao, Shun, Tang, Wu, and Yu in this present age, he would surely be mocked by a new sage. Therefore, the sage does not expect to emulate antiquity nor follow what is always acceptable; instead, he examines the circumstances of his time and prepares accordingly. A man from Song was plowing a field when he noticed a tree stump in the middle of it. A rabbit ran by, struck the stump, and broke its neck, dying instantly. The man then put down his farming tool and waited by the stump, hoping to catch another rabbit. He caught no more rabbits, but became an object of ridicule throughout the State of Song. Now, those who wish to govern the people of this age with the policies of former kings are all like the man who guarded the stump.
古者丈夫不耕，草木之實足食也；婦人不織，禽獸之皮足衣也。不事力而養足，人民少而財有餘，故民不爭。是以厚賞不行，重罰不用而民自治。今人有五子不為多，子又有五子，大父未死而有二十五孫，是以人民眾而貨財寡，事力勞而供養薄，故民爭，雖倍賞累罰而不免於亂。

In ancient times, men did not have to farm; the fruits of grass and trees were sufficient for food. Women did not weave; the hides of birds and beasts were enough for clothing. Without labor, sustenance was sufficient; with few people but abundant resources, the people did not compete. Therefore, generous rewards were unnecessary and severe punishments unused, yet the people governed themselves. Now, it is not unusual for a person to have five sons; each son may also have five sons. Before the grandfather dies, there are already twenty-five grandchildren. Thus, with so many people and few resources, labor becomes burdensome while provisions become meager, leading the people to compete. Even with doubled rewards and repeated punishments, disorder cannot be avoided.

堯之王天下也，茅茨不翦，采椽不斲，糲粢之食，藜藿之羹，冬日麑裘，夏日葛衣，雖監門之服養，不虧於此矣。禹之王天下也，身執耒臿以為民先，股無胈，脛不生毛，雖臣虜之勞不苦於此矣。以是言之，夫古之讓天子者，是去監門之養而離臣虜之勞也，古傳天下而不足多也。今之縣令，一日身死，子孫累世絜駕，故人重之；是以人之於讓也，輕辭古之天子，難去今之縣令者，薄厚之實異也。夫山居而谷汲者，膢臘而相遺以水；澤居苦水者，買庸而決竇。故饑歲之春，幼弟不饟；穰歲之秋，疏客必食；非疏骨肉愛過客也，多少之實異也。是以古之易財，非仁也，財多也；今之爭奪，非鄙也，財寡也；輕辭天子，非高也，勢薄也；爭土橐，非下也，權重也。故聖人議多少、論薄厚為之政，故罰薄不為慈，誅嚴不為戾，稱俗而行也。故事因於世，而備適於事。

When Yao ruled the world, his thatched roof was left untrimmed and his wooden beams were not carved. He ate coarse grains and drank soup made from wild vegetables. In winter he wore a fox-skin coat; in summer, hemp clothing. Even the servants at the gate received no less than this for their food and clothing. When Yu ruled the world, he personally held a plow and spade to lead the people. His thighs had no flesh left, and his shins were hairless from labor; even slaves did not endure such hardship. By this account, those in ancient times who relinquished the position of Son of Heaven were merely leaving behind the sustenance of a gatekeeper and escaping the toil of a slave. Thus, passing on the world was not considered particularly virtuous in antiquity. Nowadays, when a county magistrate dies, his descendants for generations ride in carriages and enjoy wealth; thus, people highly value such positions. Therefore, it is easy for people to relinquish the throne of an ancient Son of Heaven but difficult to give up a modern county magistrate's post; this is because the actual value and benefits differ greatly. Those who live in mountainous areas and draw water from valleys exchange water with each other during festivals. Those living near marshes, where the water is bitter, hire laborers to dig wells. Therefore, in spring during years of famine, younger brothers do not offer food to their elders. In autumn during bountiful harvests, even distant guests are sure to be fed. This is not because they love strangers more than close relatives but because the actual amount of resources available differs. Therefore, in ancient times, people's willingness to part with wealth was not due to benevolence, but because they had plenty. Nowadays, the struggle for possessions is not out of meanness, but because there is little wealth available. To easily give up the position of Son of Heaven is not a sign of lofty virtue, but due to its diminishing power; To contend for land and wealth is not a mark of low character, but because such positions carry great authority. Therefore, the sage deliberates on abundance and scarcity, considers lightness and weight in resources, and governs accordingly. Thus, lenient punishments are not signs of weakness, nor are strict punishments expressions of cruelty; they simply conform to prevailing customs and circumstances. Therefore, actions should follow the times, and preparations must suit the situation.

古者文王處豐、鎬之間，地方百里，行仁義而懷西戎，遂王天下。徐偃王處漢東，地方五百里，行仁義，割地而朝者三十有六國，荊文王恐其害己也，舉兵伐徐，遂滅之。故文王行仁義而王天下，偃王行仁義而喪其國，是仁義用於古不用於今也。故曰：世異則事異。當舜之時，有苗不服，禹將伐之，舜曰：「不可。上德不厚而行武，非道也。」乃修教三年，執干戚舞，有苗乃服。共工之戰，鐵銛矩者及乎敵，鎧甲不堅者傷乎體，是干戚用於古不用於今也。故曰：事異則備變。上古競於道德，中世逐於智謀，當今爭於氣力。齊將攻魯，魯使子貢說之，齊人曰：「子言非不辯也，吾所欲者土地也，非斯言所謂也。」遂舉兵伐魯，去門十里以為界。故偃王仁義而徐亡，子貢辯智而魯削。以是言之，夫仁義辯智，非所以持國也。去偃王之仁，息子貢之智，循徐、魯之力使敵萬乘，則齊、荊之欲不得行於二國矣。

In ancient times, King Wen resided between Feng and Hao, ruling a territory of only one hundred li. By practicing benevolence and righteousness, he won the hearts of the western Rong tribes and thus became king of all under heaven. Xu Yanwang ruled in the east of Han, governing a territory of five hundred li. Practicing benevolence and righteousness, thirty-six states ceded land to pay him homage. King Wen of Jing feared that Xu would become a threat, so he raised an army to attack Xu and eventually destroyed it. Thus, King Wen practiced benevolence and righteousness and became king of the world; Xu Yanwang did likewise but lost his state. This shows that benevolence and righteousness were effective in ancient times but not in modern times. Therefore, it is said: When the age changes, so do circumstances. In the time of Shun, the Miaos were disobedient. Yu was about to attack them, but Shun said: "No, you must not." "Without a strong moral foundation and resorting to military force is against the Way." So he refined his moral instruction for three years, holding shields and axes in dance, and thus the Miaos submitted. In the battle of Gonggong, those with sharp iron weapons reached their enemies; those with weak armor were wounded. This shows that shields and axes were effective in ancient times but are not so today. Therefore, it is said: When circumstances change, preparations must also change. In the most ancient times, people competed in virtue and morality; in the middle ages, they pursued wisdom and strategy; in our present age, competition is based on strength and power. The State of Qi was about to attack Lu, and the state sent Zi Gong to persuade them. The people of Qi said: "Your words are not lacking in eloquence, but what we desire is land; this is not something your words can address." So they raised an army to attack Lu and set their border ten li away from the city gates. Thus, Xu Yanwang practiced benevolence and righteousness yet his state perished; Zi Gong was eloquent and wise yet the State of Lu still declined. From this, it can be said that benevolence, righteousness, eloquence, and wisdom are not sufficient to preserve a state. If Xu Yanwang had abandoned benevolence and Zi Gong had ceased to rely on wisdom, but instead strengthened the military power of Xu and Lu so as to contend with a force of ten thousand chariots, then Qi and Jing would not have been able to impose their will upon these two states.

夫古今異俗，新故異備，如欲以寬緩之政、治急世之民，猶無轡策而御駻馬，此不知之患也。今儒、墨皆稱先王兼愛天下，則視民如父母。何以明其然也？曰：「司寇行刑，君為之不舉樂；聞死刑之報，君為流涕。」此所舉先王也。夫以君臣為如父子則必治，推是言之，是無亂父子也。人之情性，莫先於父母，皆見愛而未必治也，雖厚愛矣，奚遽不亂？今先王之愛民，不過父母之愛子，子未必不亂也，則民奚遽治哉！且夫以法行刑而君為之流涕，此以效仁，非以為治也。夫垂泣不欲刑者仁也，然而不可不刑者法也，先王勝其法不聽其泣，則仁之不可以為治亦明矣。且民者固服於勢，寡能懷於義。仲尼，天下聖人也，修行明道以遊海內，海內說其仁，美其義，而為服役者七十人，蓋貴仁者寡，能義者難也。故以天下之大，而為服役者七十人，而仁義者一人。魯哀公，下主也，南面君國，境內之民莫敢不臣。民者固服於勢，誠易以服人，故仲尼反為臣，而哀公顧為君。仲尼非懷其義，服其勢也。故以義則仲尼不服於哀公，乘勢則哀公臣仲尼。今學者之說人主也，不乘必勝之勢，而務行仁義則可以王，是求人主之必及仲尼，而以世之凡民皆如列徒，此必不得之數也。

Ancient and modern customs differ; new and old times require different preparations. To govern the people of a crisis-ridden age with lenient policies is like trying to control an unruly horse without reins or whip—it is a danger born from ignorance. Now, both the Confucians and Mohists claim that former kings loved all under heaven equally, regarding their people as their own children. How can this be proven? It is said: "When the official of punishment carried out executions, the ruler would not play music in mourning." "When hearing news of a capital sentence, the ruler wept bitterly." This is how they cite former kings. If the relationship between ruler and subject were truly like that of father and son, then governance would surely be orderly. By this reasoning, there could never be discord in a family. Human nature places no relationship above that of parent and child, yet even with parental love, a family is not necessarily well-ordered. Although the affection may be deep, why should disorder suddenly cease? Now, the love of former kings for their people did not exceed that of parents for their children. Yet even children may still be disorderly; how then can it be assumed that the people would suddenly become orderly? Moreover, if a ruler weeps when punishments are carried out according to law, this is merely an act of benevolence; it does not serve as effective governance. To weep and wish to avoid punishment is benevolence, yet it cannot be avoided because of the law. Former kings overcame their emotions and followed the law rather than yielding to tears; thus, it is clear that benevolence alone cannot serve as governance. Moreover, the people naturally submit to authority and rarely are moved by righteousness. Confucius was a sage of the world. By cultivating virtue and clarifying the Way, he traveled throughout the land. The people praised his benevolence and admired his righteousness; seventy disciples followed him in service. This shows that those who truly value benevolence are few, and those capable of practicing righteousness are rare. Thus, despite the vastness of the world, only seventy people followed him in service, and among them, only one was a practitioner of benevolence and righteousness. Duke Ai of Lu was an inferior ruler; yet as the sovereign seated in his court, all the people within his borders dared not fail to be his subjects. The people naturally submit to power; it is indeed easy to subdue them through authority. Thus, Confucius became a subject while Duke Ai remained the ruler. Confucius did not submit out of reverence for righteousness but because he yielded to power. Therefore, if one relies on righteousness alone, Confucius would not have submitted to Duke Ai; but through authority, Duke Ai could make Confucius his subject. Now, scholars who advise rulers insist that without relying on an invincible position of power and merely by practicing benevolence and righteousness one can become king. This is to demand that all rulers must equal Confucius and assume that the common people are all like his disciples—this is a mistaken calculation that will never succeed.

今有不才之子，父母怒之弗為改，鄉人譙之弗為動，師長教之弗為變。夫以父母之愛，鄉人之行，師長之智，三美加焉，而終不動其脛毛，不改；州部之吏，操官兵、推公法而求索姦人，然後恐懼，變其節，易其行矣。故父母之愛不足以教子，必待州部之嚴刑者，民固驕於愛、聽於威矣。故十仞之城，樓季弗能踰者，峭也；千仞之山，跛牂易牧者，夷也。故明王峭其法、而嚴其刑也。布帛尋常，庸人不釋；鑠金百溢，盜跖不掇。不必害則不釋尋常，必害手則不掇百溢，故明主必其誅也。是以賞莫如厚而信，使民利之；罰莫如重而必，使民畏之；法莫如一而固，使民知之。故主施賞不遷，行誅無赦。譽輔其賞，毀隨其罰，則賢不肖俱盡其力矣。

Now there is an unmanageable son; when his parents are angry, he does not change. When the townspeople scold him, he remains unmoved. Even when teachers instruct him, he still refuses to reform. Despite the love of his parents, the conduct of his fellow townspeople, and the wisdom of his teachers—three virtues combined upon him—he still does not stir a muscle or change. Only when the local officials, wielding official troops and enforcing public law, search for evildoers does he finally become frightened, change his conduct, and alter his behavior. Therefore, parental love alone is insufficient to teach a son; it must be supplemented by the strict punishments of local authorities. This shows that people are naturally arrogant in the face of affection but obedient when confronted with authority. Therefore, a ten-ren high wall could not be scaled by Lou Ji because it was sheer and steep; a thousand-ren tall mountain is easily climbed by a lame goat because its slopes are gentle. Therefore, wise rulers make their laws strict and their punishments severe. Common people do not let go of ordinary cloth and hemp, which are everyday items; Therefore, even if a hundred dou of molten gold were offered, the thief Dazhi would not touch it. It is because there is no danger that ordinary people do not release common goods, but if there is a risk of injury, even great wealth will be left untouched. Therefore, wise rulers must ensure their punishments are certain. Therefore, rewards should be generous and trustworthy so that the people find them beneficial; punishments must be severe and certain to instill fear in the people; laws should be uniform and firm so that the people understand them. Therefore, a ruler must bestow rewards without deviation and carry out punishments without pardon. When praise accompanies reward and censure follows punishment, then both the virtuous and the unworthy will exert their full efforts.

今則不然，以其有功也爵之，而卑其士官也；以其耕作也賞之，而少其家業也；以其不收也外之，而高其輕世也；以其犯禁也罪之，而多其有勇也。毀譽、賞罰之所加者相與悖繆也，故法禁壞而民愈亂。今兄弟被侵必攻者廉也，知友被辱隨仇者貞也，廉貞之行成，而君上之法犯矣。人主尊貞廉之行，而忘犯禁之罪，故民程於勇而吏不能勝也。不事力而衣食則謂之能，不戰功而尊則謂之賢，賢能之行成而兵弱而地荒矣。人主說賢能之行，而忘兵弱地荒之禍，則私行立而公利滅矣。

Now it is not so; when someone has achieved merit, they are granted a title but held in low esteem as an official. When someone is rewarded for farming, their family's estate is considered insignificant; when they are excluded because they do not conform to society's expectations, it is claimed that they hold the world in low regard. When someone is punished for breaking laws, it is said that they possess great courage. Thus, the application of censure and praise, rewards and punishments, becomes contradictory and erroneous; as a result, laws and prohibitions break down and the people become even more disorderly. Now, if a brother is wronged and one attacks in retaliation, it is considered upright; if a friend is insulted and one seeks revenge, it is deemed loyal. When such conduct of uprightness and loyalty becomes widespread, the laws of the sovereign are violated. When a ruler honors upright and loyal conduct but overlooks the crime of breaking laws, people measure themselves by bravery while officials cannot control them. Those who obtain food and clothing without labor are called capable; those who gain respect without military merit are considered virtuous. When such conduct of so-called virtue and capability becomes widespread, the army weakens and the land lies fallow. When a ruler praises such so-called virtue and capability but ignores the dangers of a weak army and neglected land, private conduct is encouraged while public interests are destroyed.

儒以文亂法，俠以武犯禁，而人主兼禮之，此所以亂也。夫離法者罪，而諸先生以文學取；犯禁者誅，而群俠以私劍養。故法之所非，君之所取；吏之所誅，上之所養也。法趣上下四相反也，而無所定，雖有十黃帝不能治也。故行仁義者非所譽，譽之則害功；文學者非所用，用之則亂法。楚之有直躬，其父竊羊而謁之吏，令尹曰：「殺之，」以為直於君而曲於父，報而罪之。以是觀之，夫君之直臣，父之暴子也。魯人從君戰，三戰三北，仲尼問其故，對曰：「吾有老父，身死莫之養也。」仲尼以為孝，舉而上之。以是觀之，夫父之孝子，君之背臣也。故令尹誅而楚姦不上聞，仲尼賞而魯民易降北。上下之利若是其異也，而人主兼舉匹夫之行，而求致社稷之福，必不幾矣。古者蒼頡之作書也，自環者謂之私，背私謂之公，公私之相背也，乃蒼頡固以知之矣。今以為同利者，不察之患也。然則為匹夫計者，莫如脩行義而習文學。行義脩則見信，見信則受事；文學習則為明師，為明師則顯榮；此匹夫之美也。然則無功而受事，無爵而顯榮，為有政如此，則國必亂，主必危矣。故不相容之事，不兩立也。斬敵者受賞，而高慈惠之行；拔城者受爵祿，而信廉愛之說；堅甲厲兵以備難，而美薦紳之飾；富國以農，距敵恃卒，而貴文學之士；廢敬上畏法之民，而養遊俠私劍之屬。舉行如此，治強不可得也。國平養儒俠，難至用介士，所利非所用，所用非所利。是故服事者簡其業，而游學者日眾，是世之所以亂也。

The Confucians use words to disrupt the law; the knights-errant use force to break prohibitions. Yet rulers honor both, and this is why disorder arises. Those who deviate from the law are guilty; yet many scholars gain favor through literary talent alone; those who break prohibitions should be punished, yet groups of knights-errant are supported with private swords. Thus, what the law condemns is what the ruler favors; what officials punish is what superiors support. When the law contradicts the actions of rulers and officials, with all four directions opposing one another and no fixed standard, even ten Huangdis could not bring order. Therefore, those who practice benevolence and righteousness are not to be praised; praising them harms the effectiveness of governance; those skilled in literature are not to be employed; employing them leads to disorder in the law. In the State of Chu, there was a man named Zhigong. His father stole a sheep, and he reported him to the officials. The Prime Minister said: "Execute him," arguing that while he was upright toward the ruler, he had been disrespectful to his father. He was thus punished for this act. From this example, we see that a loyal minister of the ruler may be considered an unfilial son to his father. A man from Lu fled three times in battle with the ruler's army. Confucius asked him why, and he replied: "I have an elderly father; if I die, no one will care for him." Confucius considered this filial piety and recommended him to a higher position. From this example, we see that the son who is filial to his father may be regarded as a disloyal minister to the ruler. Therefore, when the Prime Minister executed Zhigong, the unjust in Chu did not dare report their actions; but when Confucius praised him, the people of Lu became more willing to flee from battle. The interests of rulers and subjects are thus so different; yet sovereigns who simultaneously promote the conduct of commoners while seeking to secure the well-being of the state will certainly not succeed. In ancient times, when Cangjie created writing, he called a circle around oneself "si" (private), and turning away from the self "gong" (public). Thus, it was clear to Cangjie that public and private interests are opposed. To consider them as mutually beneficial now is a failure to observe carefully. Therefore, for the common person, there is no better course than cultivating virtue and righteousness while studying literature. When one cultivates virtue and righteousness, he gains trust; when trusted, he is entrusted with responsibilities; when literary learning is mastered, one becomes a respected teacher; as a respected teacher, one attains honor and distinction. This is the excellence of the common person. But if one receives responsibilities without merit and attains honor without rank, and governance is like this, then the state must fall into disorder, and the ruler will certainly be in danger. Therefore, mutually exclusive matters cannot coexist. Those who slay the enemy receive rewards, yet those with high acts of kindness and compassion are honored; those who capture cities receive ranks and emoluments, yet teachings about integrity and love are believed; armor is strengthened and weapons sharpened to prepare for difficulties, yet the adornments of scholars and officials are praised; the state grows wealthy through agriculture, resists enemies by relying on soldiers, yet values literati. They neglect the people who respect their superiors and abide by laws, while nurturing wandering knights-errant with private swords. To govern in this manner, strength and order cannot be achieved. In times of peace, Confucians and knights-errant are nurtured; in times of crisis, warriors with armor are employed. What is beneficial is not what is used, and what is used is not what brings benefit. Therefore, those who serve official duties neglect their responsibilities, while wandering scholars grow in number daily—this is why the world falls into disorder.

且世之所謂賢者，貞信之行也。所謂智者，微妙之言也。微妙之言，上智之所難知也。今為眾人法，而以上智之所難知，則民無從識之矣。故糟糠不飽者不務梁肉，短褐不完者不待文繡。夫治世之事，急者不得，則緩者非所務也。今所治之政，民閒之事，夫婦所明知者不用，而慕上知之論，則其於治反矣。故微妙之言，非民務也。若夫賢良貞信之行者，必將貴不欺之士。不欺之士者，亦無不欺之術也。布衣相與交，無富厚以相利，無威勢以相懼也，故求不欺之士。今人主處制人之勢，有一國之厚，重賞嚴誅，得操其柄，以修明術之所燭，雖有田常、子罕之臣，不敢欺也，奚待於不欺之士？今貞信之士不盈於十，而境內之官以百數，必任貞信之士，則人不足官，人不足官則治者寡而亂者眾矣。故明主之道，一法而不求智，固術而不慕信，故法不敗，而群官無姦詐矣。

Moreover, what the world calls virtuous people are those with upright and trustworthy conduct. What is called wisdom refers to subtle and refined words. Subtle and refined words are difficult even for the most intelligent minds to understand. Now, if laws for the common people rely on what is hard even for the wisest to comprehend, then the people will have no way of recognizing them. Therefore, those who are not satisfied with coarse food do not seek fine grains and meat; those whose rough clothes are incomplete do not wait for embroidered garments. In matters of governing a well-ordered society, if urgent needs cannot be met, then non-urgent concerns are not what should be pursued. Now, in the governance of state affairs and matters among the people, what husbands and wives clearly understand is disregarded, while one aspires to lofty theories known only by superiors—this leads directly away from good governance. Therefore, subtle and refined words are not what the people should pursue. If one values upright and trustworthy conduct, then he must certainly honor those who do not deceive others. Those who do not deceive are also without deceptive methods. Commoners interact with one another, neither having wealth to benefit each other nor power to intimidate; thus they seek those who do not deceive. Now, the sovereign holds authority over others and possesses the wealth of an entire state. With generous rewards and severe punishments in hand, he controls the levers of power to illuminate matters clearly through sound methods. Even if there were ministers as cunning as Tian Chang or Zi Han, they would dare not deceive him—why then should one rely on those who do not deceive? Now, upright and trustworthy men number no more than ten, while officials within the borders are counted in hundreds. If one must appoint only those who are upright and trustworthy, then there will be insufficient people to fill official posts; if there are not enough people for the offices, then those governing well will be few and those causing disorder will be many. Therefore, the way of a wise ruler is to rely on one law and not seek wisdom, to maintain firm methods without yearning for trustworthiness. Thus, laws do not fail, and all officials remain free from deceit and fraud.

今人主之於言也，說其辯而不求其當焉；其用於行也，美其聲而不責其功焉。是以天下之眾，其談言者務為辯而不周於用，故舉先王言仁義者盈廷，而政不免於亂；行身者競於為高而不合於功，故智士退處巖穴、歸祿不受，而兵不免於弱，政不免於亂，此其故何也？民之所譽，上之所禮，亂國之術也。今境內之民皆言治，藏商、管之法者家有之，而國愈貧，言耕者眾，執耒者寡也；境內皆言兵，藏孫、吳之書者家有之，而兵愈弱，言戰者多，被甲者少也。故明主用其力，不聽其言；賞其功，必禁無用；故民盡死力以從其上。夫耕之用力也勞，而民為之者，曰：可得以富也。戰之為事也危，而民為之者，曰：可得以貴也。今修文學、習言談，則無耕之勞、而有富之實，無戰之危、而有貴之尊，則人孰不為也？是以百人事智而一人用力，事智者眾則法敗，用力者寡則國貧，此世之所以亂也。故明主之國，無書簡之文，以法為教；無先王之語，以吏為師；無私劍之捍，以斬首為勇。是境內之民，其言談者必軌於法，動作者歸之於功，為勇者盡之於軍。是故無事則國富，有事則兵強，此之謂王資。既畜王資而承敵國之舋，超五帝，侔三王者，必此法也。

Now, when a sovereign hears words, he delights in eloquence without seeking whether they are appropriate; when it comes to action, he admires the reputation of an individual without demanding results. Therefore, among the people of the world, those who speak are devoted to eloquence without practical use. Hence, even though the court is filled with discussions about benevolence and righteousness from past sage kings, governance cannot avoid disorder; those who cultivate their conduct compete in appearing lofty without aligning with actual achievements. Thus, wise men withdraw to remote caves and refuse official salaries, yet the military cannot avoid weakness, and governance remains no less disorderly. What is the reason for this? What the people praise, what superiors honor—this is the method of a state in chaos. Now, within the realm all the people speak of good governance; every household claims to possess the laws of Shang Yang and Guan Zhong, yet the state becomes poorer—many talk about farming, but few actually hold plows. Within the realm all speak of military affairs; every household claims to have the writings of Sun Tzu and Wu Qi, yet the army becomes weaker—many talk about war, but few don armor. Therefore, a wise ruler uses people's efforts rather than listening to their words; he rewards achievements and must prohibit uselessness; thus, the people exert their utmost strength to follow their ruler. Farming requires hard labor, yet people do it because they say: "It can bring wealth." War is a dangerous endeavor, yet people engage in it because they say: "It can bring honor and rank." Now, by cultivating literary learning and engaging in eloquent discourse, one avoids the labor of farming yet gains its rewards; one avoids the dangers of war yet attains honor. Who would not do this? Therefore, a hundred people pursue intellect while only one labors physically. When those pursuing intellect are numerous, the law fails; when those laboring physically are few, the state becomes poor—this is why the world descends into disorder. Therefore, in a country ruled by a wise sovereign, there are no writings on bamboo slips; law serves as education; there is no discourse about past sage kings; officials serve as teachers; there are no private swords for defense; beheading the enemy is considered bravery. Thus, within the realm, those who speak must conform to law; those who act direct their efforts toward achievements; and those who seek bravery dedicate themselves fully to the military. Therefore, in times of peace the state is wealthy, and in times of war the army is strong—this is called the foundation for becoming a hegemon. Having accumulated such resources and seizing opportunities from rival states, one who surpasses the Five Emperors and rivals the Three Sovereigns must follow this method.

今則不然，士民縱恣於內，言談者為勢於外，外內稱惡以待強敵，不亦殆乎！故群臣之言外事者，非有分於從衡之黨，則有仇讎之忠，而借力於國也。從者，合眾弱以攻一強也；而衡者，事一強以攻眾弱也；皆非所以持國也。今人臣之言衡者皆曰：「不事大則遇敵受禍矣。」事大未必有實，則舉圖而委，效璽而請兵矣。獻圖則地削，效璽則名卑，地削則國削，名卑則政亂矣。事大為衡未見其利也，而亡地亂政矣。人臣之言從者皆曰：「不救小而伐大則失天下，失天下則國危，國危而主卑。」救小未必有實，則起兵而敵大矣。救小未必能存，而交大未必不有疏，有疏則為強國制矣。出兵則軍敗，退守則城拔，救小為從未見其利，而亡地敗軍矣。是故事強則以外權士官於內，救小則以內重求利於外，國利未立，封土厚祿至矣；主上雖卑，人臣尊矣；國地雖削，私家富矣。事成則以權長重，事敗則以富退處。人主之於其聽說也，於其臣，事未成則爵祿已尊矣；事敗而弗誅，則游說之士，孰不為用矰繳之說而徼倖其後？故破國亡主以聽言談者之浮說，此其故何也？是人君不明乎公私之利，不察當否之言，而誅罰不必其後也。皆曰「外事大可以王，小可以安。」夫王者，能攻人者也；而安，則不可攻也。強，則能攻人者也；治，則不可攻也。治強不可責於外，內政之有也。今不行法術於內，而事智於外，則不至於治強矣。鄙諺曰：「長袖善舞，多錢善賈。」此言多資之易為工也。故治強易為謀，弱亂難為計。故用於秦者十變而謀希失，用於燕者一變而計希得，非用於秦者必智，用於燕者必愚也，蓋治亂之資異也。故周去秦為從，期年而舉；衛離魏為衡，半歲而亡。是周滅於從，衛亡於衡也。使周、衛緩其從衡之計，而嚴其境內之治，明其法禁，必其賞罰，盡其地力以多其積，致其民死以堅其城守，天下得其地則其利少，攻其國則其傷大，萬乘之國、莫敢自頓於堅城之下，而使強敵裁其弊也，此必不亡之術也。舍必不亡之術而道必滅之事，治國者之過也。智困於內而政亂於外，則亡不可振也。

Now, however, scholars and commoners indulge within the state; those who speak seek influence abroad. Internally and externally, they foster hostility toward a powerful enemy—would this not be perilous! Therefore, when officials speak of foreign affairs, they are either aligned with factions advocating alliances or enmity, or they feign loyalty to rivals while seeking strength for the state. Alliance (cong) means uniting many weak states to attack one strong power; while balancing (heng) means serving one strong state to attack the many weak ones; neither is a proper way to preserve the state. Now, those officials who advocate balancing (heng) all say: "If we do not serve a great power, we will face enemies and suffer disaster." Serving a great power may not necessarily yield results; thus, they submit maps to surrender territory and offer seals while requesting troops. Offering maps leads to the loss of land; offering seals results in a lowered status. Losing land weakens the state, and a lowered status brings disorder to governance. Serving a great power as balancing (heng) has not yet shown benefits, but it already causes the loss of territory and disorder in governance. Those officials who advocate alliance (cong) all say: "If we do not rescue the small and attack the great, we will lose the world; losing the world means national peril, and national peril leads to a ruler's humiliation." Rescuing the small may not yield real results, yet it incites war against a great power. Saving the small does not necessarily preserve them; allying with the great may still lead to estrangement. If estranged, one will be controlled by a powerful state. Marching out leads to military defeat; retreating and defending results in the loss of cities. Rescuing small states through alliance (cong) has not shown benefits, yet it causes territorial losses and military failure. Therefore, when serving a strong power, officials within the state gain influence through foreign alliances; when rescuing small states, they seek benefits abroad by leveraging domestic authority. Before national interests are secured, large fiefs and generous salaries already arrive; although the ruler is humiliated, officials become respected; although state territory is reduced, private families grow wealthy. If the matter succeeds, they gain power and prestige; if it fails, their wealth allows them to retreat in comfort. The sovereign, regarding what he hears and believes about his officials, bestows ranks and emoluments of high status even before their affairs are completed; if they fail yet escape punishment, then which wandering orator would not employ deceptive arguments in the hope of later fortune? Therefore, why do rulers who listen to empty words from eloquent speakers end up with ruined states and lost thrones? What is the reason for this? The reason lies in their failure to distinguish between true merit and hollow rhetoric. It is because the sovereign does not discern the interests of public versus private matters, fails to examine whether words are appropriate or not, and does not ensure that punishments follow inevitably. All say: "Dealing with external affairs on a grand scale can lead to hegemony; on a smaller scale, it ensures stability." A hegemon is one who can attack others; while stability means being unassailable. Strength enables one to attack others; order makes one unassailable. Order and strength cannot be obtained from external sources; they arise from internal governance. chluss If within the state one does not apply law and technique, yet seeks wisdom externally, then order and strength will never be achieved. A vulgar proverb says: "Long sleeves are good for dancing; much money is good for trade." This means that having abundant resources makes it easy to excel in one's craft. Therefore, when a state is well-governed and strong, plans are easily made; but when weak and in disorder, strategies become difficult to formulate. Thus, those serving the State of Qin could change their plans ten times and rarely fail in strategy; while those serving Yan changed once and seldom succeeded. This is not because those who served Qin were necessarily wise or those who served Yan were foolish—it was due to differences in the resources available from order and disorder. Therefore, when Zhou left Qin to join an alliance (cong), within a year it collapsed; when Wei left the State of Wei to adopt balancing (heng), half a year later it perished. Thus, Zhou was destroyed by alliance (cong) and Wei perished through balancing (heng). If Zhou and Wei had delayed their strategies of alliance or balancing, instead strictly governing within their borders, clarifying laws and prohibitions, ensuring clear rewards and punishments, fully utilizing the productivity of their land to increase their reserves, and inspiring their people with a willingness to die for defense so as to strengthen city fortifications—then even if other states gained their territory, they would gain little benefit; attacking their countries would cause great damage. No major power (with ten thousand chariots) would dare to halt its forces before strong walls or allow powerful enemies to exploit their weaknesses. This is the sure way to avoid destruction. To abandon a strategy that ensures survival and instead pursue actions leading inevitably to ruin—this is the fault of those who govern states. When wisdom is trapped within internal affairs and governance is in chaos externally, then destruction cannot be averted.

民之故計，皆就安利如辟危窮。今為之攻戰，進則死於敵，退則死於誅則危矣。棄私家之事而必汗馬之勞，家困而上弗論則窮矣。窮危之所在也，民安得勿避。故事私門而完解舍，解舍完則遠戰，遠戰則安。行貨賂而襲當塗者則求得，求得則私安，私安則利之所在，安得勿就？是以公民少而私人眾矣。夫明王治國之政，使其商工游食之民少而名卑，以寡趣本務而趨末作。今世近習之請行則官爵可買，官爵可買則商工不卑也矣；姦財貨賈得用於市則商人不少矣。聚斂倍農而致尊過耕戰之士，則耿介之士寡而高價之民多矣。

The people's natural inclination is to seek safety and benefit while avoiding danger and hardship. Now, if they are forced into war, advancing means death at the hands of the enemy, retreating means death by punishment—this is perilous indeed. Abandoning private family affairs to endure the hardships of military service, yet with families in hardship and superiors offering no consideration—this leads to destitution. Where there is poverty and peril, how can the people avoid fleeing? Therefore, those who serve private families complete their dwellings; when dwellings are completed, they engage in distant warfare; and through distant warfare, safety is achieved. Those who offer bribes and infiltrate positions of power obtain their desires; when desires are obtained, private interests are secured. When private interests are secure, that is where benefits lie—how can one avoid pursuing them? Therefore, the number of loyal citizens decreases while the number of self-serving individuals increases. The governance of a wise ruler in managing the state ensures that merchants, artisans, and idlers are few in number and hold low status, so as to reduce their pursuit of secondary occupations and encourage them instead toward fundamental duties. In the present age, when requests from those close to power are heeded, official ranks and titles can be purchased. When official ranks and titles can be bought, then merchants and artisans no longer hold low status; when illicit wealth is used in the marketplace, there will certainly be many merchants. When those who amass wealth surpass farmers in accumulation and attain respect exceeding that of soldiers and warriors, then upright individuals become few while people seeking high status through wealth multiply.
是故亂國之俗，其學者則稱先王之道，以籍仁義，盛容服而飾辯說，以疑當世之法而貳人主之心。其言古者，為設詐稱，借於外力，以成其私而遺社稷之利。其帶劍者，聚徒屬，立節操，以顯其名而犯五官之禁。其患御者，積於私門，盡貨賂而用重人之謁，退汗馬之勞。其商工之民，修治苦窳之器，聚弗靡之財，蓄積待時而侔農夫之利。此五者，邦之蠹也。人主不除此五蠹之民，不養耿介之士，則海內雖有破亡之國，削滅之朝，亦勿怪矣。

Therefore, in a state in disorder, its scholars cite the ways of ancient kings and invoke benevolence and righteousness, displaying elaborate attire and eloquent arguments to cast doubt on current laws and confuse the ruler's mind. Those who speak of antiquity fabricate deceptions, cite external forces, and pursue private gain at the expense of the state's interests. Those who wear swords gather followers and establish moral standards to display their fame, yet they violate official prohibitions. Those who seek favor accumulate at private households, exhausting wealth and bribes to gain the recommendation of powerful individuals, thus displacing those who have labored in military service. The merchants and artisans produce crude, poorly made goods, amass wealth without extravagance, and store it for the right moment to compete with farmers in profit. These five groups are pests to the state. If a ruler does not eliminate these five groups of harmful people and fails to nurture upright individuals, then even if there are within the realm states that fall into ruin or dynasties that perish, it should come as no surprise.
